claim: Lipid turnover is generally accepted to be rapid.
source: Lipids are critical to cellular function and it is generally accepted that lipid turnover is rapid and dysregulation in turnover results in disease (Dawidowicz 1987; Phillips et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Dawidowicz 1987; Phillips et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2013) and represents established scientific consensus.

claim: Dysregulation in lipid turnover results in disease.
source: Lipids are critical to cellular function and it is generally accepted that lipid turnover is rapid and dysregulation in turnover results in disease (Dawidowicz 1987; Phillips et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Dawidowicz 1987; Phillips et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2013).

claim: In the center of the human ocular lens, there is no lipid turnover in fiber cells during the entire human lifespan.
source: In this study, we present an intriguing counter-example by demonstrating that in the center of the human ocular lens, there is no lipid turnover in fiber cells during the entire human lifespan.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by radiocarbon dating measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are pronounced changes in lens lipid composition over a lifetime.
source: This discovery, combined with prior demonstration of pronounced changes in the lens lipid composition over a lifetime (Hughes et al., 2012), suggests that some lipid classes break down in the body over several decades, whereas others are stable.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Hughes et al., 2012).

claim: Some lipid classes break down in the body over several decades, whereas others are stable.
source: This discovery, combined with prior demonstration of pronounced changes in the lens lipid composition over a lifetime (Hughes et al., 2012), suggests that some lipid classes break down in the body over several decades, whereas others are stable.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combination of no lipid turnover and observed changes in lipid composition.

claim: Substantial changes in lens cell membranes may play a role in the genesis of age-related eye disorders.
source: Such substantial changes in lens cell membranes may play a role in the genesis of age-related eye disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications of the findings.

claim: Whether long-lived lipids are present in other tissues is not yet known.
source: Whether long-lived lipids are present in other tissues is not yet known, but this may prove to be important in understanding the development of age-related diseases.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Long-lived lipids may prove to be important in understanding the development of age-related diseases.
source: Whether long-lived lipids are present in other tissues is not yet known, but this may prove to be important in understanding the development of age-related diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future implications.

claim: The membrane lipid composition of most tissues is dynamic and alters within days in response to diet.
source: The membrane lipid composition of most tissues is dynamic and alters within days in response to diet (Katan et al., 1997; Owen et al., 2004) and weeks in response to exercise (Mitchell et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Katan et al., 1997; Owen et al., 2004).

claim: The membrane lipid composition of most tissues alters within weeks in response to exercise.
source: The membrane lipid composition of most tissues is dynamic and alters within days in response to diet (Katan et al., 1997; Owen et al., 2004) and weeks in response to exercise (Mitchell et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Mitchell et al., 2004).

claim: Cellular phospholipid turnover can be detected within minutes after intravenous injection of fatty acids.
source: Indeed, cellular phospholipid turnover can be detected within minutes after intravenous injection of fatty acids (Thies et al., 1994; Shetty et al., 1996; Rapoport et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Thies et al., 1994; Shetty et al., 1996; Rapoport et al., 1997).

claim: In tissues where access to the metabolic machinery for membrane renewal is restricted, it is possible that some lipids are longer lived.
source: However, in tissues where access to the metabolic machinery for membrane renewal is restricted, it is possible that some lipids are longer lived but this has never been shown.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on restricted metabolic access, but noted as previously undemonstrated.

claim: Long-lived lipids have never been shown to exist prior to this study.
source: However, in tissues where access to the metabolic machinery for membrane renewal is restricted, it is possible that some lipids are longer lived but this has never been shown.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the state of prior knowledge.

claim: If long-lived lipids are present, the properties of the tissues in which they are incorporated may be influenced by the decomposition or modification of the lipidome over time.
source: If long-lived lipids are present, the properties of the tissues in which they are incorporated may be influenced by the decomposition or modification of the lipidome over time.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences of long-lived lipids.

claim: There is no cellular turnover in the human lens.
source: There is no cellular turnover in the human lens (Lynnerup et al., 2008) and its center—a region known as the nucleus—is devoid of cellular organelles (Bassnett and Beebe, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Lynnerup et al., 2008).

claim: The center of the human lens, a region known as the nucleus, is devoid of cellular organelles.
source: There is no cellular turnover in the human lens (Lynnerup et al., 2008) and its center—a region known as the nucleus—is devoid of cellular organelles (Bassnett and Beebe, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Bassnett and Beebe, 1992).

claim: Accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) was utilized to measure carbon-14 (14C) levels in lipids extracted from the human lens nucleus of donors covering a range of birth dates from 1948 to 1993.
source: In this study, accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) was utilized to measure carbon-14 (14C) levels in lipids extracted from the human lens nucleus of donors covering a range of birth dates from 1948 to 1993.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Above-ground testing of nuclear weapons occurred from 1955 until 1963.
source: This approach exploits the global pulse of artificial atmospheric 14CO2 resulting from above-ground testing of nuclear weapons that occurred from 1955 until 1963 (Libby et al., 1964; Harkness and Walton, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Libby et al., 1964; Harkness and Walton, 1972).

claim: The concentration of 14C has decreased exponentially from 1963 until the present day due to the exchange of atmospheric CO2 in the oceans and biosphere.
source: The concentration of 14C has decreased exponentially from 1963 until the present day due to the exchange of atmospheric CO2 in the oceans and biosphere.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about atmospheric 14C dynamics.

claim: The lens grows continuously throughout life by the addition of fiber cells to a pre-existing lens that was present at birth (the nucleus).
source: The lens grows continuously throughout life by the addition of fiber cells to a pre-existing lens that was present at birth (the nucleus) (Lynnerup et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Lynnerup et al., 2008).

claim: In the absence of turnover of cellular components, the 14C level of an individual's lens nucleus reflects the 14C abundance of the year in which they were born.
source: Therefore, in the absence of turnover of cellular components, the 14C level of an individual's lens nucleus reflects the 14C abundance of the year in which they were born.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the principles of radiocarbon dating and lens growth.

claim: If turnover occurs rapidly, 14C abundance reflects current levels present in the atmosphere.
source: If turnover occurs rapidly, 14C abundance reflects current levels present in the atmosphere, while an intermediate value would suggest a slower rate of exchange.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on radiocarbon dating principles.

claim: An intermediate 14C value would suggest a slower rate of exchange.
source: If turnover occurs rapidly, 14C abundance reflects current levels present in the atmosphere, while an intermediate value would suggest a slower rate of exchange.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on radiocarbon dating principles.

claim: Measurement of the amount of 14C present in a class of biomolecules allows the determination of the date of biosynthesis and the time the system ceased exchanging carbon with its surroundings, or the rate of exchange with its surroundings.
source: Given this information, measurement of the amount of 14C present in a class of biomolecules allows the determination of the date of biosynthesis and the time the system ceased exchanging carbon with its surroundings, or the rate of exchange with its surroundings.
evidence: This is established knowledge about radiocarbon dating methodology.

claim: Nuclei were carefully dissected from individual human lenses of 23 donors of known birth dates.
source: We carefully dissected nuclei from individual human lenses of 23 donors of known birth dates.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure performed in the study.

claim: The average human lens nucleus is approximately 6–7 mm in diameter.
source: The average human lens nucleus is approximately 6–7 mm in diameter (Hermans et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Hermans et al., 2007).

claim: A cylinder of 4.5 mm in diameter was cut in the axial plane using a trephine to avoid contamination of fiber cells laid down postnatally.
source: Therefore, to avoid contamination of fiber cells laid down postnatally, we cut a cylinder of 4.5 mm in diameter in the axial plane using a trephine, then removed 1 mm from either end as previously described (Friedrich and Truscott, 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and its rationale.

claim: 1 mm was removed from either end of the lens nucleus cylinder.
source: Therefore, to avoid contamination of fiber cells laid down postnatally, we cut a cylinder of 4.5 mm in diameter in the axial plane using a trephine, then removed 1 mm from either end as previously described (Friedrich and Truscott, 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, with citation to prior methodology (Friedrich and Truscott, 2009).

claim: The Folch method reports high yield of lipids and minimal protein contamination.
source: Total lipids present in each lens nucleus were obtained using a well-established method that reports high yield of lipids and minimal protein contamination (Folch et al., 1957).
evidence: Supported by citation to the Folch method (Folch et al., 1957).

claim: Protein is the major component of lenses by mass.
source: Since protein is the major component of lenses by mass and lens proteins are known to be present since birth (Stewart et al., 2013), the residual protein content of lipid extracts was determined using a standard BCA assay (Smith et al., 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge about lens composition.

claim: Lens proteins are known to be present since birth.
source: Since protein is the major component of lenses by mass and lens proteins are known to be present since birth (Stewart et al., 2013), the residual protein content of lipid extracts was determined using a standard BCA assay (Smith et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Stewart et al., 2013).

claim: Residual protein was found to represent less than 0.5% of the total weight of carbon in the extract.
source: Residual protein was found to represent less than 0.5% of the total weight of carbon in the extract, and therefore a negligible contribution to the 14C measurement.
evidence: This is a measurement result from the study.

claim: Residual protein represents a negligible contribution to the 14C measurement.
source: Residual protein was found to represent less than 0.5% of the total weight of carbon in the extract, and therefore a negligible contribution to the 14C measurement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured low protein content.

claim: Radiocarbon content in lens lipids was found to closely match the atmospheric levels of the date of birth.
source: Radiocarbon content in lens lipids was determined by AMS and was found to closely match the atmospheric levels of the date of birth (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The fraction of 14C present in the lipid extract from a human lens nucleus was found to be a highly accurate predictor of the year of birth (R2 = 0.9683).
source: As shown in Figure 1B, the fraction of 14C (f14C) present in the lipid extract from a human lens nucleus was found to be a highly accurate predictor of the year of birth (R2 = 0.9683), indicating negligible lipid turnover during the human lifespan.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The high correlation between 14C fraction and year of birth indicates negligible lipid turnover during the human lifespan.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, the fraction of 14C (f14C) present in the lipid extract from a human lens nucleus was found to be a highly accurate predictor of the year of birth (R2 = 0.9683), indicating negligible lipid turnover during the human lifespan.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the high correlation observed in the data.

claim: The values obtained for f14C for human lens nuclear lipids are consistent with previous reports on the f14C for insoluble protein fraction.
source: The values obtained for f14C for human lens nuclear lipids (and thus a predictor of the year of birth) obtained in the present study are consistent with previous reports on the f14C for insoluble protein fraction (Stewart et al., 2013) and total protein (Lynnerup et al., 2008) of the human lens nucleus.
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior literature (Stewart et al., 2013).

claim: The values obtained for f14C for human lens nuclear lipids are consistent with previous reports on the f14C for total protein of the human lens nucleus.
source: The values obtained for f14C for human lens nuclear lipids (and thus a predictor of the year of birth) obtained in the present study are consistent with previous reports on the f14C for insoluble protein fraction (Stewart et al., 2013) and total protein (Lynnerup et al., 2008) of the human lens nucleus.
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior literature (Lynnerup et al., 2008).

claim: Radiocarbon dating has been previously utilized to examine the longevity of tooth enamel.
source: Although radiocarbon dating has been previously utilized to examine the longevity of human tissues (e.g., tooth enamel [Spalding et al., 2005] and lenses [Lynnerup et al., 2008]) and biomolecules (e.g., insoluble proteins [Stewart et al., 2013] and DNA [Bhardwaj et al., 2006; Spalding et al., 2008; Bergmann et al., 2009]), the results presented here are the first demonstration of the existence of long-lived lipids in any animal.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Spalding et al., 2005).

claim: Radiocarbon dating has been previously utilized to examine the longevity of lenses.
source: Although radiocarbon dating has been previously utilized to examine the longevity of human tissues (e.g., tooth enamel [Spalding et al., 2005] and lenses [Lynnerup et al., 2008]) and biomolecules (e.g., insoluble proteins [Stewart et al., 2013] and DNA [Bhardwaj et al., 2006; Spalding et al., 2008; Bergmann et al., 2009]), the results presented here are the first demonstration of the existence of long-lived lipids in any animal.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Lynnerup et al., 2008).

claim: Radiocarbon dating has been previously utilized to examine the longevity of insoluble proteins.
source: Although radiocarbon dating has been previously utilized to examine the longevity of human tissues (e.g., tooth enamel [Spalding et al., 2005] and lenses [Lynnerup et al., 2008]) and biomolecules (e.g., insoluble proteins [Stewart et al., 2013] and DNA [Bhardwaj et al., 2006; Spalding et al., 2008; Bergmann et al., 2009]), the results presented here are the first demonstration of the existence of long-lived lipids in any animal.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Stewart et al., 2013).

claim: Radiocarbon dating has been previously utilized to examine the longevity of DNA.
source: Although radiocarbon dating has been previously utilized to examine the longevity of human tissues (e.g., tooth enamel [Spalding et al., 2005] and lenses [Lynnerup et al., 2008]) and biomolecules (e.g., insoluble proteins [Stewart et al., 2013] and DNA [Bhardwaj et al., 2006; Spalding et al., 2008; Bergmann et al., 2009]), the results presented here are the first demonstration of the existence of long-lived lipids in any animal.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Bhardwaj et al., 2006; Spalding et al., 2008; Bergmann et al., 2009).

claim: The results presented here are the first demonstration of the existence of long-lived lipids in any animal.
source: Although radiocarbon dating has been previously utilized to examine the longevity of human tissues (e.g., tooth enamel [Spalding et al., 2005] and lenses [Lynnerup et al., 2008]) and biomolecules (e.g., insoluble proteins [Stewart et al., 2013] and DNA [Bhardwaj et al., 2006; Spalding et al., 2008; Bergmann et al., 2009]), the results presented here are the first demonstration of the existence of long-lived lipids in any animal.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the study, supported by the radiocarbon dating data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The lack of molecular turnover in the human lens lipidome may be due to its unique pattern of growth.
source: The lack of molecular turnover in the human lens lipidome may be due to its unique pattern of growth.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed findings.

claim: The lens grows continuously throughout life and pre-existing cells are encapsulated by newly formed fiber cells.
source: The lens grows continuously throughout life and pre-existing cells are encapsulated by newly formed fiber cells (Bassnett and Beebe, 1992) such that the adult lens nucleus is comprised of cells biosynthesized in utero.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Bassnett and Beebe, 1992).

claim: The adult lens nucleus is comprised of cells biosynthesized in utero.
source: The lens grows continuously throughout life and pre-existing cells are encapsulated by newly formed fiber cells (Bassnett and Beebe, 1992) such that the adult lens nucleus is comprised of cells biosynthesized in utero.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of lens growth described in the cited literature.

claim: The composition of human lens membranes is quite different from those of other mammals.
source: The composition of human lens membranes is quite different from those of other mammals (Borchman et al., 2004), possibly reflecting our long lifespan.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Borchman et al., 2004).

claim: The difference in human lens membrane composition possibly reflects our long lifespan.
source: The composition of human lens membranes is quite different from those of other mammals (Borchman et al., 2004), possibly reflecting our long lifespan.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed compositional differences.

claim: In human lenses, sphingomyelins are more abundant than glycerophospholipids.
source: In human lenses, sphingomyelins are more abundant than glycerophospholipids (Borchman et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Borchman et al., 1994).

claim: Sphingomyelins have been discovered intact in a 40,000-year-old woolly mammoth.
source: The chemical stability of sphingomyelins is illustrated by the fact that they have been discovered, intact in a 40,000-year-old woolly mammoth (Kreps et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Kreps et al., 1979).

claim: The discovery of intact sphingomyelins in a 40,000-year-old woolly mammoth illustrates the chemical stability of sphingomyelins.
source: The chemical stability of sphingomyelins is illustrated by the fact that they have been discovered, intact in a 40,000-year-old woolly mammoth (Kreps et al., 1979).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited finding about woolly mammoth sphingomyelins.

claim: The higher degree of saturation found in sphingomyelins present in the human lens (i.e., predominantly dihydrosphingomyelins) may confer unique chemical and physical stability to the membranes of lens fiber cells.
source: Furthermore, the higher degree of saturation found in sphingomyelins present in the human lens (i.e., predominantly dihydrosphingomyelins), may confer unique chemical and physical stability to the membranes of lens fiber cells (Yappert and Borchman, 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to prior literature (Yappert and Borchman, 2004).

claim: The data obtained here on lipid longevity are consistent with the results of quantitative molecular analysis of lipids isolated from human lens nuclei of different ages.
source: The data obtained here on lipid longevity are consistent with the results of quantitative molecular analysis of lipids isolated from human lens nuclei of different ages.
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior studies.

claim: The total amount of glycerophospholipid classes such as phosphatidylcholines and phosphatidylethanolamines was found to decrease significantly with age.
source: In these studies, the total amount of glycerophospholipid classes such as phosphatidylcholines and phosphatidylethanolamines was found to decrease significantly with age, whereas the content of dihydrosphingomyelin and sphingomyelin remained relatively stable (Hughes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Hughes et al., 2012).

claim: The content of dihydrosphingomyelin and sphingomyelin remained relatively stable with age.
source: In these studies, the total amount of glycerophospholipid classes such as phosphatidylcholines and phosphatidylethanolamines was found to decrease significantly with age, whereas the content of dihydrosphingomyelin and sphingomyelin remained relatively stable (Hughes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Hughes et al., 2012).

claim: The age-related changes in lipid content reflect the relative chemical stability of the different lipid classes under the conditions experienced within the lens over a lifetime.
source: Presumably, these results reflect the relative chemical stability of the different lipid classes under the conditions experienced within the lens over a lifetime.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed age-related changes in lipid composition.

claim: Some cells contain long-lived lipids.
source: These findings reveal that some cells contain long-lived lipids and this discovery may have significant implications for other post-mitotic cells.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the radiocarbon dating data.

claim: The discovery of long-lived lipids may have significant implications for other post-mitotic cells.
source: These findings reveal that some cells contain long-lived lipids and this discovery may have significant implications for other post-mitotic cells.

claim: The slope of the correlation between predicted year of birth and actual year of birth was approximately one (0.98 ± 0.04).
source: The slope was approximately one (0.98 ± 0.04) and the y-intercept was indistinguishable from zero within the measured error (39 ± 75).

claim: The y-intercept of the correlation between predicted year of birth and actual year of birth was indistinguishable from zero within the measured error (39 ± 75).

evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The lipid samples closely match the levels of artificial 14CO2 present in the atmosphere in the northern hemisphere and southern hemisphere from 1950 until 1990.
source: The lipid samples (•) are superimposed over the levels of artificial 14CO2 present in the atmosphere in the northern hemisphere (light gray) and the southern hemisphere (dark gray) from 1950 until 1990 (Hua et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown visually in Figure 1A where the data points align with the atmospheric curves.

claim: Typical sample sizes for 14C/12C isotopic ratio measurements were in the range of 70–120 μg of carbon.
source: Typical sample sizes were in the range of 70–120 μg of carbon.
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters used in the study.

claim: The STAR accelerator has greater than 0.5% precision for samples above 50 μg.
source: 14C/12C isotopic ratios were measured on the Small Tandem for Applied Research (STAR) accelerator, which has greater than 0.5% precision for samples above 50 μg.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the instrument used.

claim: Blanks produced a residual solvent carbon mass of 10–20 μg following evaporation.
source: Blanks produced a residual solvent carbon mass of 10–20 μg following evaporation and were measured for radiocarbon on the Australian National Tandem for Applied Research (ANTARES) accelerator (Fink et al., 2004), which provides greater accuracy for samples less than 50 μg carbon.
evidence: This describes the experimental results for blank samples.

claim: The ANTARES accelerator provides greater accuracy for samples less than 50 μg carbon.
source: Blanks produced a residual solvent carbon mass of 10–20 μg following evaporation and were measured for radiocarbon on the Australian National Tandem for Applied Research (ANTARES) accelerator (Fink et al., 2004), which provides greater accuracy for samples less than 50 μg carbon.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the instrument, supported by citation (Fink et al., 2004).

claim: Calendar dates were obtained by calibrating the radiocarbon determinations with the online version of the CALIbomb software using the southern hemisphere data sets for the bomb pulse.
source: Calendar dates were obtained by calibrating the radiocarbon determinations with the online version of the CALIbomb software (14CHRONO Centre of the Queen's University of Belfast, 2014) using the southern hemisphere data sets for the bomb pulse (Hua et al., 2013) and the tree ring southern hemispheric curve for data points prior to the 1950s (Hogg et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology, supported by citations to the software and calibration datasets.

claim: A small enrichment in δ13C was observed at −22.7 ± 0.1 and −21.2 ± 0.7‰ for unlabeled and labeled solvents, respectively.
source: While both δ13C results were in the normal range of −20 to −24‰, a small enrichment was observed at −22.7 ± 0.1 and −21.2 ± 0.7‰ for unlabeled and labeled solvents, respectively.
evidence: This is a measurement result from the solvent retention experiment.

claim: If the observed δ13C values represent isotopic exchange or retention of solvent by lipids, the carbon weight fraction of this contamination would be ∼0.013%.
source: Should these values represent isotopic exchange or retention of solvent by lipids, the carbon weight fraction of this contamination would be ∼0.013% and is therefore negligible.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured δ13C values.

claim: The carbon weight fraction of potential solvent contamination (∼0.013%) is negligible.
source: Should these values represent isotopic exchange or retention of solvent by lipids, the carbon weight fraction of this contamination would be ∼0.013% and is therefore negligible.
